## Tulsa race massacre 1921 main article English Wikipedia summary
# Tulsa Race Massacre (May 31 – June 1, 1921) — Summary of English Wikipedia Main Article

**Source:** [1] English Wikipedia article *"Tulsa race massacre"* (long titled *"Tulsa race riot"*; retitled to reflect the consensus of historians and institutions). Key references within it include the 2001 Oklahoma Commission report, Scott Ellsworth's *Death in a Promised Land*, and Alfred Brophy's scholarship.

## Overview
A two-day attack by a white mob on the Greenwood District of Tulsa, Oklahoma — one of the wealthiest Black communities in the U.S., nicknamed "Black Wall Street." It is regarded as one of the worst single incidents of racial violence in American history and was omitted from local and state histories for decades.

## Background & Trigger
- Greenwood, founded 1906, had ~10,000 residents by 1921 amid Tulsa's oil-boom segregation (Jim Crow); tensions included lynchings and a resurgent Ku Klux Klan.
- May 30, 1921: Dick Rowland, a Black shoeshiner, had an elevator encounter with Sarah Page, a white elevator operator, in the Drexel Building; he was arrested May 31 on an assault allegation.
- A sensational *Tulsa Tribune* report (the page is now lost) allegedly inflamed a lynch threat; a white mob gathered at the courthouse while Black men, including WWI veterans, arrived to protect Rowland.

## The Violence
- Shots were fired at the courthouse the evening of May 31; outnumbered Black defenders retreated to Greenwood.
- Overnight and into June 1, white rioters looted and systematically burned ~35 blocks of Greenwood.
- Martial law was declared and National Guard troops restored order by midday June 1.
- Private aircraft were used for reconnaissance; claims of gunfire from planes remain disputed.

## Casualties & Damage
- Official death toll: 36 (26 Black, 10 white); historians estimate 75–300, with the American Red Cross estimating up to 300 [1].
- ~1,256 homes burned and 215 looted; ~10,000 people left homeless; hospital, churches, schools, and businesses destroyed; property damage ~$1.5–2 million in 1921 dollars.
- Up to ~6,000 Black residents were detained for days in camps (Convention Hall, fairgrounds, McNulty Park), requiring ID cards to leave.

## Aftermath
- No white rioters were prosecuted; a grand jury largely blamed the Black community. Charges against Rowland were dismissed in September 1921 after Page declined to press charges.
- A city fire ordinance blocking rebuilding was struck down by the Oklahoma Supreme Court; insurance claims were largely denied. Greenwood was substantially rebuilt by the mid-1920s, later declining from urban renewal and highway construction (I-244).
- The NAACP's Walter F. White investigated; W.E.B. Du Bois covered it in *The Crisis*.

## Legacy
- The 2001 Oklahoma Commission report recommended reparations that were never enacted. Renewed attention came via HBO's *Watchmen* (2019) and the 2021 centennial, when President Biden visited Tulsa.
- Mass-grave searches at Oaklawn Cemetery began in 2020; the first victim, WWI veteran C.L. Daniel, was identified in 2024.
- A reparations lawsuit (Lessie Benningfield Randle et al. v. City of Tulsa) was dismissed, with the Oklahoma Supreme Court declining review in June 2024 [1].

---

## Tulsa race massacre 1921 causes and events Greenwood district
# Tulsa Race Massacre (May 31 – June 1, 1921)

## The Greenwood District ("Black Wall Street")
- Developed in north Tulsa after 1906, when Black entrepreneur O.W. Gurley bought 40 acres and sold plots to Black settlers; segregation laws confined Tulsa's Black residents there, concentrating wealth and commerce [1][2].
- By 1921, roughly 10,000–12,000 Black Tulsans lived in Greenwood, supporting dozens of Black-owned businesses, two newspapers (the *Tulsa Star* and *Oklahoma Sun*), hotels (including the Stradford Hotel), doctors' and lawyers' offices, churches, a hospital, and schools. It was reportedly dubbed "Negro Wall Street" by Booker T. Washington [1][3][5].

## Causes
- **Jealousy and racial resentment** of Greenwood's prosperity in a booming, segregated oil town [1][4].
- **Post-WWI racial tension**: Black veterans returning with assertiveness, the "Red Summer" race riots of 1919, and a growing Ku Klux Klan presence (Tulsa Klan membership surged to ~3,200 by late 1921) [1][3].
- **A lynching culture**: the August 1920 lynching of white murder suspect Roy Belton from courthouse grounds, with police inaction, signaled mob violence would go unpunished [1].
- **The trigger**: On May 30, 1921, Dick Rowland, a 19-year-old Black shoeshiner, entered an elevator in the Drexel Building operated by 17-year-old white elevator operator Sarah Page. He apparently tripped and grabbed her arm; she screamed, a clerk assumed an assault, and Rowland was arrested May 31 [1][2].
- **Inflammatory press**: A May 31 *Tulsa Tribune* article on the arrest, plus an alleged editorial ("To Lynch Negro Tonight" — the page is missing from archives), helped draw a white mob demanding Rowland's lynching [1][4].
- **Official complicity**: Police deputized hundreds of white men, some of whom participated in the violence; the sheriff, by contrast, barricaded the jail and refused mob demands [1][3].

## Events
- **May 31, evening**: A mob of ~2,000 whites gathered at the courthouse. Around 9 p.m., ~25 armed Black men, many WWI veterans, offered to help protect Rowland and were turned away. A second group of ~75 arrived around 10 p.m.; when a white man tried to seize a Black man's gun, a shot fired and the riot began [1][2].
- Black defenders retreated to Greenwood as the mob grew; whites attempted to storm the National Guard armory but were repelled [1].
- **June 1, ~1 a.m.**: Fires began on Greenwood's northern edge; by dawn, organized, partly "deputized" white crowds invaded the district, looting and burning systematically. Six or more private planes circled overhead for reconnaissance; eyewitnesses (e.g., attorney B.C. Franklin) reported incendiaries being dropped, though this remains debated [1][4].
- Renowned Black surgeon A.C. Jackson was shot dead while surrendering [1].
- **~11:30 a.m. June 1**: Governor James B.A. Robertson declared martial law; National Guard troops from Oklahoma City restored order. Martial law was lifted June 4 [1][3].
- **Internment**: Up to 6,000 Black residents were detained at Convention Hall, the fairgrounds, and McNulty Park, released over days with ID cards and white escorts [1][2].

## Casualties and Destruction
- Official 1921 death count: 36; the 2001 Oklahoma Commission estimated 100–300 killed (Red Cross estimated up to 300) [1].
- ~35 blocks destroyed; 1,256 homes burned and 215 looted; hundreds of businesses, 12 churches, a hospital, and both newspapers' offices destroyed; ~10,000 left homeless [1][2][5].
- Insurance claims were denied under "riot" exclusion clauses [1].

## Aftermath and Legacy
- A grand jury largely blamed Greenwood's Black residents; charges against Rowland were dropped in September 1921 after Page declined to prosecute [1][3].
- A city zoning ordinance intended to block rebuilding was struck down by the Oklahoma Supreme Court (1922); Greenwood was rebuilt by 1925 and peaked in the 1940s, before decline from desegregation and I-244's construction through the district in the late 1960s–70 [1][5].
- Long suppressed as a "riot," it was renamed a "massacre" in recent years; the 2001 state commission recommended reparations; a survivors' reparations lawsuit was dismissed by the Oklahoma Supreme Court in June 2024. Excavations at Oaklawn Cemetery (2020–2024) have recovered remains from mass graves [6][7][8].

## Sources
[1] Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921, final report (2001)
[2] Tulsa Historical Society & Museum, "The 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre"
[3] Oklahoma Historical Society, *Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture* — "Tulsa Race Massacre"
[4] Smithsonian Magazine, coverage including B.C. Franklin's eyewitness account
[5] National Museum of African American History and Culture (Smithsonian), "1921 Tulsa Race Massacre"
[6] Associated Press, coverage of the June 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court reparations ruling
[7] City of Tulsa, 1921 Graves Investigation (Oaklawn Cemetery)
[8] 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre Centennial Commission materials (2021)

## Tulsa race massacre 1921 casualties death toll and aftermath reparations
# Tulsa Race Massacre (May 31 – June 1, 1921): Death Toll, Casualties, and Reparations

## Death toll
- **Official 1921 count: 36 deaths** (26 Black, 10 white), per Oklahoma vital statistics records [1][3].
- **American Red Cross** field report estimated **up to 300 dead** [2].
- The **2001 Oklahoma Commission** report concluded **100–300 were killed**, with ~300 plausible [1].
- **Mass grave investigations**: Excavations at Tulsa's Oaklawn Cemetery since 2020 have exhumed roughly 60 sets of remains; only a few have been identified. The first confirmed victim, **C.L. Daniel** (a Black WWI veteran), was identified in **July 2024** via DNA/genealogy work; identification efforts continue [8].

## Physical and human toll
- ~**35 square blocks** of the Greenwood district ("Black Wall Street") destroyed; **1,250+ homes** burned, plus businesses, churches, a school, and a hospital [1].
- ~**10,000 Black residents left homeless**; roughly **6,000 detained** in internment camps (Convention Hall, fairgrounds, McNulty Park) [1].
- Property damage estimated at **$1.5–2 million in 1921 dollars** (tens of millions today) [1].

## Aftermath (1920s–20th century)
- **No white perpetrators were prosecuted**; a 1921 grand jury largely blamed the Black community. Charges against Dick Rowland, whose arrest triggered the violence, were dropped in September 1921 [1].
- **~$1.8 million in insurance claims** were denied under riot-exclusion clauses, upheld by the Oklahoma Supreme Court in 1926 (*Redfearn v. American Central Ins. Co.*) [1].
- A city fire ordinance initially blocked rebuilding; Greenwood was rebuilt but later gutted by "urban renewal" and interstate construction (I-244) in the 1950s–60s [1].

## Reparations efforts
- **1997–2001**: State commission recommended direct payments to survivors/descendants, scholarships, a memorial, and Greenwood economic development. The legislature's 2001 Reconciliation Act funded scholarships and the John Hope Franklin Reconciliation Park (2010) — **but no direct payments** [1].
- **2003**: Federal suit (*Alexander v. Oklahoma*) dismissed on statute-of-limitations grounds; Supreme Court declined review in 2005 [4].
- **2020–2024**: Last survivors' suit (Lessie Benningfield Randle, Viola Fletcher, Hughes Van Ellis) sought a reparations fund via public-nuisance claims. The **Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed it in June 2024** [5]. Van Ellis died in October 2023; Fletcher and Randle remain among the last living survivors.
- **January 2025**: The **DOJ closed its first-ever federal civil rights review**, concluding the attack was coordinated and systematic but that no living perpetrators could be prosecuted [6].
- **June 2025**: Tulsa's first Black mayor, Monroe Nichols, announced a **"Road to Repair"** plan centered on a private **Greenwood Trust** (reported ~$105 million goal) for housing, scholarships, and investment — notably **excluding direct cash payments** to survivors, drawing criticism from some advocates [7].
- **No direct government reparations have ever been paid** to survivors or descendants as of late 2025; President Biden's June 1, 2021 centennial visit did not produce federal compensation [1][5][7].

---
**Sources**
[1] Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921, final report (2001)
[2] American Red Cross relief report (Maurice Willows, 1921)
[3] Oklahoma Board of Vital Statistics death records (1921)
[4] *Alexander v. Oklahoma* (10th Cir. 2004; cert. denied 2005)
[5] *Randle et al. v. City of Tulsa*, Oklahoma Supreme Court (June 2024)
[6] U.S. DOJ Civil Rights Division, review findings (January 2025)
[7] City of Tulsa "Road to Repair"/Greenwood Trust announcement (June 2025)
[8] City of Tulsa 1921 Graves Investigation updates, Oaklawn Cemetery (2020–2024)
